title: The First Job of Every Newly Promoted Leader and Successor
author: Admired Leadership
summary: Admired Leadership challenges the standard advice that a newly promoted leader should first listen to the team and survey the current reality. The more urgent first job, it argues, is retaining the talent of colleagues who wanted the role and did not get it, since they are usually capable, respected and carry institutional knowledge. Left unattended, their disappointment hardens into quiet withdrawal: they hold back ideas and wait for the new leader to stumble. The piece warns that giving them space is a mistake because avoidance reads as indifference or triumph. The better move is to approach them first, privately and early, name the situation plainly, ask for their support and then seek their counsel on a hard problem. Handled well, a former rival becomes an ally and a source of truth, and the leader earns legitimacy from above and below.
points: The first priority for a newly promoted leader is retaining the people who wanted the role, not collecting team feedback about current reality.
Passed-over candidates rarely quit loudly; they withdraw effort by degrees and withhold their best ideas.
Giving a disappointed colleague space is a mistake because they read avoidance as indifference or triumph.
The remedy is to go first, privately and early, acknowledge the situation, ask for support and then seek counsel on a hard problem.
How a leader treats a former rival signals character to the whole team, and turning a rival into a partner builds legitimacy.
quotes: They must retain the talents of those who wanted the role but didn’t get it.
These passed-over candidates seldom storm out. They withdraw their effort by degrees, withhold their best ideas, and wait for the new leader to stumble.
How the new leader treats a former rival is read as a signal of character, and it tells everyone what kind of leadership they can expect.
The instinct of many new leaders is to give the disappointed colleague space, assuming time will soften the blow. This is a mistake.
The better move is to go to them first, privately and early, and acknowledge the situation plainly. Tell them you want their support and need their help to succeed.
Respect, not reassurance, is what keeps the talented but disappointed colleague engaged.
Listening to the team matters, but the first conversation that shapes a good leader’s tenure is the one with the person who hoped to be sitting in the chair.
